claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by a balance among magnetically driven phase transformations, polymorphism, and deformation twinning.
Temperature, stress, and composition can modulate this balance.
The proposed initial material state is an as-cast or annealed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy.
Controlled temperature and stress during in situ TEM will produce or reveal microstructural evolution involving phase transformations, deformation twinning, and polymorphism.
The hypothesis is intended to apply under high-temperature, cryogenic, and irradiated conditions.
Magnetically driven phase transformations contribute to the proposed phase-stability mechanism.
Polymorphism contributes to the proposed phase-stability mechanism.
Deformation twinning contributes to the proposed phase-stability mechanism.

The balance among phase stability, microstructure, and mechanical properties determines whether desirable high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness are retained.
The proposed baseline is an as-cast or annealed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy without controlled temperature and stress conditions.
The hypothesis may not apply to high-entropy alloy systems outside Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
A controlled comparison across different compositions and processing conditions can test relationships among microstructural evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties.
Failure to observe a correlation between microstructural evolution and the predicted mechanical outcomes would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the hypothesis to a specific composition, although no specific composition is given, while the experiment proposes comparisons among different compositions.
